speaker_role: student (current international undergraduate at University of Chicago)
commercial_incentive: sponsored by Notion (mentions and links a free Notion template); no service selling beyond that
key_insights: Explains the F1 visa is a non-immigrant student visa tied to the length of one's degree program, and it assumes the student intends to return home after graduating.
Outlines the sequence: get accepted, get enrolled in SEVP, receive the physical I-20 form (needed for border crossings), pay the SEVIS fee, then schedule an embassy visa interview.
Recommends using trackable shipping for the I-20 after her own I-20 was misrouted to the wrong country and delayed her process by about three months.
Explains students can only start the Social Security Number process once employed, and on-campus jobs (through the university) are available immediately, unlike off-campus work.

Distinguishes OPT (up to 12 months of post-graduation work authorization tied to one's major) from CPT (paid/unpaid internships tied to a required or credit-bearing course), noting a student must be enrolled one full year before qualifying for either.
Notes many employers ask upfront whether an applicant needs visa sponsorship, which she says reduces international students' hiring chances since sponsorship is a hassle/cost for companies.
Advises waiving the university's often-expensive health insurance in favor of a cheaper external plan if the university allows a waiver process.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker states the SEVIS fee for F1 visas is $350 (one-time).
Speaker states her university's own insurance (UChicago) cost about $1,400/quarter (over $4,000/year), versus roughly $800/year for a third-party plan (PSI insurance, Ruby plan) she used instead.
Speaker says the overall visa process (I-20 receipt through visa issuance) typically takes about three months.
Speaker states OPT provides up to 12 months of work authorization total (not necessarily consecutive) after one year of enrollment.
notable_or_distinctive: Practical step-by-step logistics for international students (visa, insurance, SSN, OPT/CPT) told through a personal horror story about a misrouted I-20 document, rather than generic cultural-adjustment advice.
reliability_notes: This is administrative/visa logistics from a single student's personal experience, not admissions strategy; some details (e.g., in-person visa pickup policies) are noted by the speaker herself as uncertain due to COVID-era changes, and rules may have changed since this ~4-year-old video.
